figures.label: Figure 1
figures.caption: 3DCodeVerse’s showcases. Assets are built only by code (e.g., Blender Python, Three.js, and OpenGL), ranging from 3D objects to articulated objects, scenes, and graphics renderings.
figures.headline: Code alone produces 3D objects, articulated objects, scenes and graphics across Blender Python, Three.js and OpenGL.
citing_sentences: To bridge these gaps, we introduce 3DCodeVerse (Figure 1), an open-source foundational framework for learning and scaling 3D coding through a large-scale executable code corpus and a 3D code generation harness.

figures.label: Figure 2
figures.caption: Curation and composition of 3DCodeVerse-2M. Left: We collect programs from public datasets and generate more with our harness. Middle: Our 3D coding harness, equipped with modeling skills and inspection tools (e.g., 3D IoU, collision checks), builds each program, judges the output, and refines it until it passes. Each verified program is paired with rendered images and captions, plus meshes and videos when available. Right: The resulting corpus covers 3D objects, articulated objects, scenes, and graphics across multiple programming languages and engines.
figures.headline: The corpus combines public collections with harness-generated programs, each verified program paired with renders and captions.
citing_sentences: Figure 2 shows representative sources; Appendix B.2 summarizes the full collection.

figures.label: Figure 3
figures.caption: Overview of the 3DCodeVerse Harness. Given an input prompt, an LLM planner defines the target asset, and a DAG coordinates sub-agents to code and assemble a 3D program (left). Execution checks, spatial measurements, and rubric-guided VLM judgments provide automated feedback (center) for targeted code revisions by a fix agent (bottom). The right panel illustrates successive refinement rounds, with the highest-scoring program selected as the final output.
figures.headline: A planner, sub-agents and three feedback types drive refinement rounds, with the highest-scoring program selected as output.
citing_sentences: To address this bottleneck, we develop 3DCodeVerse Harness, a multi-agent framework that automates 3D code generation and refinement for data curation and agent-driven content creation (Figure 3).

figures.label: Figure 4
figures.caption: Main results of 3DCodeVerse Harness across four 3D coding tasks. Panels show (a) 3D objects, (b) articulated objects, (c) scenes, and (d) graphics. Blue bars report Human Preference (%), and orange bars report Judge Score (0–100; failed generations receive a score of zero). Hatched bars denote each backbone’s native harness, while solid bars denote 3DCodeVerse Harness. The final group in (a) compares Claude Design with 3DCodeVerse Harness, both using Claude Opus 5.5.
figures.headline: Native harnesses are rarely preferred, while each backbone within 3DCodeVerse Harness wins most human comparisons across four tasks.
citing_sentences: Figure 4 shows a consistent pattern across backbones and tasks: outputs from the native harness are rarely preferred, while the same backbone within 3DCodeVerse Harness wins most comparisons.
Table 13 reports the exact numerical values underlying Figure 4a–c alongside the VLM Preference and SigLIP-2 text–image similarity metrics.

figures.label: Figure 5
figures.caption: Qualitative comparisons and automated refinement. (a) Outputs for identical prompts and backbones using the native harness (Without) versus 3DCodeVerse Harness (With). (b) Selected rounds of automated refinement for objects and graphics. Numbers report rubric scores on a $[0,1]$ scale and are comparable within each pair or refinement sequence.
figures.headline: Harness outputs show more complete structures and finer details than native outputs, and refinement rounds fix specific defects.
citing_sentences: We report the execution rate (Table 2) and fidelity to the target (Table 6): F@0.05 between the generated and reference meshes, and DINOv2-L similarity between clay renders of the two meshes from four fixed views; failed programs score zero on both.
For matched prompts and backbones, Figure 6(a) shows that 3DCodeVerse Harness produces more complete structures and finer details, such as the phoenix’s legs and nest and the piano’s interior.

Figure 6(b) shows how successive refinement rounds correct specific defects, improving the phoenix’s facial feathers, attaching the stool legs to the seat, and reducing block artifacts in the neon shader.

figures.label: Figure 7
figures.caption: Applications. Code renders from our harness guide video generation with Gemini Omni Flash 1.1 for robot manipulation scenes (top) and Seedance 2.5 for a GPT-6 Astra scene (bottom).
figures.headline: Paired frames compare rendered code scenes with video generator outputs for robot manipulation and a GPT-6 Astra scene.

figures.label: Figure 8
figures.caption: Components and model roles. A planner, a judge, and a coding agent are configured modularly per run; the harness orchestrates stage progression, iterative refinement, and candidate selection while providing deterministic spatial tools, verification gates, multi-view renderers, and rubric aggregation. Agent programs execute across seven isolated language runtimes; dashed circles indicate pluggable model interfaces.
figures.headline: A planner, a coding agent and a vision-language judge are configured as separate pluggable roles within each run.
citing_sentences: Each run decouples structural planning, code synthesis, and visual evaluation into three pluggable roles: a planner, a coding agent, and a vision–language judge (Figure 8).

figures.label: Figure 9
figures.caption: From structural plan to file scopes and coding sessions, illustrated on the recorded trajectory of §A.6. The planner decomposes the prompt into named parts with metric bounding boxes, materials, attachment relations, and an acceptance checklist; each target maps to its owned source files, and refinement tasks sharing files are grouped into file-disjoint sessions. In Round 1, nine revision tasks partition into eight file-disjoint groups; in Round 2, four tasks form four groups.
figures.headline: Planned parts map to owned source files, and Round 1's nine revision tasks split into eight file-disjoint groups.
citing_sentences: Objects with eight or more top-level parts in modular languages are synthesized via scoped sessions over attachment subtrees of at most three parts—each supplied with the planned bounding boxes of adjacent parts—followed by an assembly session (Figure 9).

figures.label: Figure 10
figures.caption: Observations, deterministic gates, and authoring-frame feedback. A measured geometric defect is returned as a structured negative verdict rather than a protocol error (left); a single verification routine serves simultaneously as an interactive agent tool, an end-of-round gate, and a generator of prioritized revision tasks (middle). Right: baseline-round diagnostics from §A.6, with corrective translation vectors projected directly into the agent’s native authoring frame.
figures.headline: Measured defects return as negative verdicts, and corrective translations are given in each runtime's authoring frame.
citing_sentences: Although exported meshes are evaluated in the canonical Y-up frame, all corrective fix hints are projected back into each runtime’s native authoring frame: a seat floating by $12$ mm receives a corrective translation of $(0,0,-0.012)$ m in Z-up Blender Python and $(0,-0.012,0)$ m in Y-up Three.js (Figure 10).

figures.label: Figure 11
figures.caption: Vision–language judgment: evidence payload, structured schema, and score synthesis. The judge inspects structured telemetry and labelled multi-view montages without access to source code or generator reasoning (left); its schema enforces explicit visual observation prior to criterion scoring (middle). Right: baseline-round score computation for §A.6, combining criterion means, majority-voted defects, and deterministic gate caps.
figures.headline: The judge sees telemetry and multi-view montages without source code, and scores are combined with defect votes and gate caps.
citing_sentences: A single payload builder serves in-loop refinement, post-run evaluation, and judge calibration (Figure 11).

figures.label: Figure 12
figures.caption: Recorded trajectory for the prompt “a three-legged wooden stool” on the Three.js runtime under the economy profile. Each column shows one round: the rendered view inspected by the judge, the composite score with its penalties and caps, deterministic gate findings, and VLM defect votes. Closed-loop refinement resolves all baseline floating and interpenetrating parts in Round 1 ($0.410\to 0.844$) and refines geometric detailing in Round 2 ($11{,}052$ triangles, reaching $0.933$ under the strict metric-footprint cap), completing in $4.0$ active minutes at \$0.74.
figures.headline: A stool run's composite score rises from 0.410 to 0.844 in Round 1, then reaches 0.933 in Round 2.
citing_sentences: Figure 12 traces a complete run for the prompt “a three-legged wooden stool” on the Three.js runtime under the economy profile.

figures.label: Figure 13
figures.caption: Articulated mechanism verification, illustrated on a recorded run for “a laptop with a hinged lid”. Link geometry is authored in Blender and kinematic structure in URDF; the build verifies rest-pose frame agreement, and the joint sweep articulates the mechanism across its motion limits. The dynamic sweep automatically detects a subtle $2.5$ mm hinge–base collision at the upper opening limit that is invisible at rest, enforcing physical articulability via the rubric cap.
figures.headline: A dynamic joint sweep detects a 2.5 mm hinge-base collision at the upper limit that is invisible at rest.
citing_sentences: The articulated track coordinates two coupled source representations (Figure 13): a Blender Python script authoring one mesh per link in world coordinates at the rest pose, and a URDF specification placing each link frame at its kinematic pivot.

figures.label: Figure 14
figures.caption: Scene and procedural graphics tracks. (a) Scene generation executes a staged asset-and-zone assembly pipeline before entering the closed-loop refinement cycle with scene-specific gates. (b) Graphics generation synthesizes fragment shaders or OpenGL programs whose temporal frames are sampled at fixed timestamps, verified by statistical frame gates, and evaluated as multi-frame montages.
figures.headline: Scene assembly and graphics frame sampling each feed track-specific gates before the closed-loop refinement cycle.
citing_sentences: Scene synthesis executes a staged hierarchical pipeline prior to the main refinement loop (Figure 14a).

On the graphics track, the agent authors either a Shadertoy-style GLSL fragment shader (with optional multipass feedback buffers) or a moderngl Python program defining setup and per-frame render routines, while the harness injects standardized headers, uniforms, outputs, and brief-matched reference recipes (Figure 14b).

figures.label: Figure 15
figures.caption: Training loss dynamics of the three Qwen3.8-27B data-scale runs. (a) Cross-entropy loss per optimizer step; faint curves show raw 5-step logs and solid curves show an exponential moving average ($\tau=50$ steps). (b) Smoothed loss trajectories plotted against epoch fraction to align cosine learning-rate schedules, annotated with terminal smoothed losses. Each trajectory tracks in-distribution optimization across its respective representation mixture from $293$ K to $1.99$ M rows.
figures.headline: All three Qwen3.8-27B data-scale runs converge smoothly, with no logged step above 1.3× the trailing 20-step average.
citing_sentences: Figure 15 demonstrates smooth, stable convergence across all three regimes: no logged step exceeds $1.3\times$ the trailing $20$-step moving average, and all runs are entirely free of instability or divergence spikes.

figures.label: Figure 16
figures.caption: Articulated code simulation vs. UWM rollouts on the generated asset (Initial State 1). Rows correspond to contact push, hold, and retreat control sequences ($16$ commands at $20$ Hz). Columns show the initial observation, MuJoCo simulation of the generated 3D code, its reconstruction through UWM’s frozen VAE, the static last-frame reference, and all three UWM rollout seeds. Enlarged $2\times$ crops (dashed boxes) demonstrate that executable 3D code preserves sharp, consistent door and handle geometry both before and after VAE reconstruction, whereas UWM rollouts exhibit seed-dependent contour drift.
figures.headline: Simulated code preserves door and handle geometry before and after VAE reconstruction, while video-model rollouts drift across seeds.
citing_sentences: Table 17 and Figures 16–17 clarify the structural advantage of programmatic 3D assets for embodied simulation.

figures.label: Figure 17
figures.caption: Articulated code simulation vs. UWM rollouts on the generated asset (Initial State 2). Control sequences, column layout, and fixed $2\times$ crops match Figure 16, displaying all nine UWM rollouts for Initial State 2.
figures.headline: Figure 17 shows all nine video-model rollouts for Initial State 2 beside the simulated code.
citing_sentences: Table 17 and Figures 16–17 clarify the structural advantage of programmatic 3D assets for embodied simulation.

abstract: We introduce 3DCodeVerse, a research ecosystem that enables coding agents to create editable and verifiable 3D content at scale. 3DCodeVerse comprises large-scale, high-quality datasets of executable 3D code, a coding harness for spatial reasoning and automated verification, and practical guidance for 3D coding. First, we construct 3DCodeVerse-2M, a large-scale curated dataset of standalone 3D executable code. We build this corpus by collecting open-source data, converting specialized representations, and generating new programs with coding agents. Each program is packaged with the source files and associated assets required for execution in its declared environment, along with available descriptions and verification records. Second, we develop the 3DCodeVerse Harness, a multi-agent directed acyclic graph framework for generating and refining 3D content. It uses execution checks, spatial measurements, and visual feedback to automatically evaluate and revise generated programs without human feedback during generation. Third, we conduct systematic empirical studies of 3D coding, establishing baselines with fine-tuned open models and deriving practical guidance through component-level analyses of our harness. Extensive experiments demonstrate that fine-tuning on our dataset significantly improves the 3D coding capabilities of open-source models. Notably, our 3DCodeVerse harness achieves a 90% win rate against Claude Design (3D Object) in pairwise human evaluations, when both are utilized by Claude Opus 5.5.

sections.body: The introduction argues that shared infrastructure for 3D coding is limited, and that Table 1 shows existing datasets mainly cover static or articulated objects. The paper introduces **3DCodeVerse-2M**, a corpus of standalone executable 3D programs converted from heterogeneous representations and paired with assets, descriptions and verification signals. It also introduces the **3DCodeVerse Harness**, which generates and revises programs through execution, spatial and visual checks without human feedback during generation. Stated results: execution rates of 84.9% with a 9B model and 92.9% with a 27B model on 3DCodeBench, and gains of 15.5–29.1 points over one-shot generation for coding agents.
sections.heading: Introduction
sections.headline: 3DCodeVerse combines a curated executable 3D code dataset with a harness that verifies and revises generated programs.

sections.body: The related work groups prior resources into datasets and benchmarks, and harnesses. Datasets cover CAD construction sequences (DeepCAD, Fusion 360 Gallery), executable CadQuery and Blender programs (BlendNet, CAD-Recode, MeshCoder), and procedural assets and shaders (Infinigen, Shaders21k). Harnesses use execution and visual feedback (SceneCraft, LL3M, VIGA, Articraft). The authors state that their focus is scaling executable supervision across heterogeneous coding environments. Their harness is positioned as reusable across coding backends and as a data engine that generates, refines and filters training programs without human feedback in the curation loop. The section reports no measured comparison.
sections.heading: Related Work
sections.headline: Prior 3D code work covers datasets, benchmarks and feedback harnesses, but these remain fragmented across tasks and environments.

sections.body: The section defines 3D coding as writing a program that builds 3D content meeting a condition in a declared environment, where execution yields an artifact and feedback: $(a,\ell)=\mathcal{E}_{e}(f)$. Success requires executability and high-quality content. Sources include public resources (Bioinspired3D, 3DCodeBench, Thingiverse, Shadertoy), DeepCAD sequences converted to CadQuery, Articraft geometry with its URDF retained, a ProcTHOR subset, and harness-generated programs. Conversion fidelity is measured by voxel IoU for DeepCAD and Chamfer distance for Articraft. Each record stores provenance, license and verification results. Coverage varies by source, and harness-generated programs also carry gate and judge results as quality tiers.
sections.heading: 3DCodeVerse-2M: A large-scale 3D coding dataset
sections.headline: 3DCodeVerse-2M packages standalone executable 3D programs with assets, captions and separate verification records.

sections.body: The harness generates 3D programs from text, images or videos without human feedback during a run. An LLM planner produces a plan with components, dimensions, materials and acceptance criteria, which is translated into a directed acyclic graph of coding and assembly tasks run by sub-agents. Each round collects three feedback types: build logs, measurement checks for dimensions, contacts and collisions, and a VLM judge scoring multi-view renders against criteria. Feedback becomes revision tasks applied by a fix agent. A development-time adversarial loop alternates refining the judge and the generation workflow, using a consistency objective for judge variance and for contradictions with measurements. The section reports no numeric evaluation.
sections.heading: 3DCodeVerse Harness: A Data Engine for 3D Coding
sections.headline: The harness uses a multi-agent graph with execution, spatial and visual feedback to revise programs without human input.

sections.body: Evaluation compares outputs from each backbone's native harness with 3DCodeVerse Harness on 100 object prompts, plus articulated, scene and graphics prompts, using Human Preference, VLM Preference and a Judge Score from 0 to 100. On 3D objects, Human Preference for the harness ranges from 69% to 89%, and Judge Score improves by 11–25 points; Gemini 3.8 Flash rises from 61 to 87. Against Claude Design, both using Claude Opus 5.5, the harness wins 90% of human comparisons with a Judge Score of 88 versus 37. For fine-tuning, LoRA on 3DCodeVerse-2M raises execution on 3DCodeBench from 0.0 to 84.9 for Qwen3.5-9B and from 51.9 to 92.9 for Qwen3.8-27B. Table 2 decoding uses one seed.
sections.heading: Experiments
sections.headline: Harness outputs win most human comparisons, reaching 90% against Claude Design, and fine-tuning raises execution rates.

sections.body: Two applications are described. For robotics, a door-and-handle asset validated with 3DCodeVerse tools was imported into MuJoCo and compared with frozen predictions from a video world-action model (UWM) across 12 cases with two assets, two contact states and three control sequences. Code renders and their VAE reconstructions passed the fixed geometry check in 12/12 outputs, versus 7/36 UWM predictions. For video generation, rendered 3D scenes serve as reference videos conditioning Gemini Omni Flash and Seedance 2.5. Paired frames are shown to examine preservation of layout, object motion and camera trajectories. The video results are presented as frames, with no numeric measure.
sections.heading: Applications of 3D coding
sections.headline: Code renders pass a door-and-handle geometry check in 12/12 outputs, versus 7/36 for a frozen video world-action model.

sections.body: The conclusion summarizes 3DCodeVerse as an open ecosystem with datasets, a reusable harness and open model baselines. It states that the dataset gathers programs across environments with descriptions, assets and quality records, and that the harness supports iterative generation without human feedback during a run while keeping programs and revisions for curation. It cites experiments showing that the data helps train open models and that the harness benefits existing coding agents. The authors state that they will release the datasets, harness, models and training recipes to support further research on 3D generation through code.
sections.heading: Conclusion
sections.headline: The authors plan to release datasets, harness, models and training recipes after reporting open-model and harness results.

sections.body: The appendix documents the harness: seven isolated runtimes across four tracks, planner, coding agent and judge roles, file-scoped subtree decomposition, deterministic gates, and rubric aggregation with vetoes. It also gives a recorded three-legged stool run, articulated-object checks, and scene and graphics track descriptions. Table 17 ablations report that a context reset cut the plan-stage failure rate by 6.7× (13/277 to 2/276, p=0.0067), and that separating verdicts from transport errors reduced redundant retries by 20× across 3,677 invocations. Halving turn depth cut cumulative session tokens by 68%. Appendix D compares executable code with a frozen video model on 12 cases.
sections.heading: Appendix
sections.headline: The appendix details harness runtimes, planning, judge scoring, a recorded run, articulation checks and a video-model comparison.
